messages.subject: Example models, visually
messages.body_plain:
I almost have the next shinyStan ready, and I think we should host shinyStan versions of some of the example models and other useful models for instructing people on stan-users. We can link to them from the manual and/or example models pages, and especially when relevant questions are asked on the message board. Then users can look at the code and also explore the model visually (they can see the Stan code in shinyStan too), and they can do this immediately, without having to organize, compile or fit the model. I think this would be really helpful, both for users and for us answering questions.

We could do all this easily using shinyapps.io <http://shinyapps.io>. It would be free if a bunch of us rotated hosting them on the more limited unpaid accounts (some loyal users might also offer to host some), but we might have to keep changing the links. Alternatively, the cheapest paid plan is $40/month, but that would give us plenty of usage hours.

Jonah

Port shouldn't matter, as to host multiple apps they should (probably) sit behind nginx or some other reverse proxy anyway.

The dilemma with shinyapps IMO, is I don't understand what they mean by 'active-hours' in their pricing model. Even if they aggresively spin up/down instances, as the popularity/interest of stan grows, if people are casually pinging the examples it will very quickly exhaust those hours if it is a binary on/off for the calculation vs actual resource consumption.

There are some cool possibilities with solutions like https://sandstorm.io/ and using docker sandboxes, however I'm still in the experimenting, so I can't make any production-ready recommendations for a couple more weeks.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
I'm playing around with some ideas for transforming Stan programs and perhaps doing auto-differentiation via source code transformation instead of via operator overloading. C++ isn't the best language for that sort of symbolic computing, so I'm looking at other languages more suited to the task. At some point I'll probably want to contribute the code to Stan, which means that accessibility and familiarity to the Stan development team are important criteria in choice of language.

Mathematica is probably the best language for implementing these kinds of transformations, but it fails on accessibility -- it has a hefty licensing fee. The possibilities I'm considering are Haskell, Common Lisp, Racket (a dialect of Scheme), F#, Clojure, OCaml, Standard ML, and Scala. My question to you all is this: which of these languages, if any, are you comfortable with?

That'd be a rather different approach of doing a symbolic derivative.
That is, you'd generate an expression, then differentiate using SymPy,
then code up the resulting expression.  Theano uses symbolic math for
derivatives, and it's in Python, so you could also look there.

You'll have much more luck finding people comfortable with Python than
any of the others you mention.

The alternative tha I thought Kevin was suggesting was to just
code generate the autodiff.  There are a bunch of autodiff systems
that do that for (subsets of) Fortran and C (not C++).  You could
even write a C++ system that ran once to record the expression then
took a pass over the abstract syntax tree to code generate the
derivative.  That's how I'd approach the problem if we needed to do
it within Stan.

Matt Hoffman was urging us to look at both this kind of approach
and the Theano symbolic differentiation approach all along.  It's much
more work than autodiff, though, because you can't autodiff through
complex iterative functions like we used to do.

messages.body_plain:
> Even for a simple model it hits its maximum number of iterations with the default arguments
That’s… rather unfortunate. I think for such simple models, this can easily be solved by doing the adaptation of the learning rate hyperparameter as Andrew mentioned. Alp and I are working on that now. The general idea is to write this as part of a new “warm up” stage for ADVI. Not sure when we’ll get it done.

>  Is there some guidance as to what "INSPECT ELBO" entails?

This warning occurs whenever the change in the ELBO is too large—greater than a constant threshold. It might signify that the gradients are blowing up and thus the optimization routine is not converging. This almost always occurs at the beginning of ADVI, which is not surprising because changes in the ELBO are expected to be drastic in the beginning. Unfortunately, we haven’t found a good heuristic to make that threshold be large in the beginning so that such warnings aren’t outputted, and then have it decrease over time; the problem is equivalent to trying to predict the progress of the optimization within some “window". For now we leave the threshold as a constant.

> But in my opinion MCSE, N_Eff, N_Eff/s, and R_hat should not appear in the VB output because the samples are iid.

Yeah, I don’t think these make much sense in the context of approximate inference yet. The only reason they exist at the moment is because they’re required for the output functions.
* MCSE is a bit pointless for variational inference because we may as well write down the analytic variance coming from the variational distribution instead.
* Getting estimates for N_Eff and N_eff/s for a posterior approximation sounds really really hard. It’s also not well-posed what this means in the context of analytic approximating distributions (VB) rather than empirical distributions (MCMC). I think this needs to be studied more closely first.
* Same as above for R_hat, which Andrew, Alp and I would like to work on soon.

> The "Samples were drawn using meanfield with ." thing is messed up in CmdStan.

Thanks for the heads-up. I’ll submit an issue for this in CmdStan.

Dustin

On the other hand, we could cache the best ELBO evaluation. But either seems better than taking a chance that the last state is randomly awful and then letting the user make inferences from the result.

Generally I would agree although we have to be a bit careful about this. This is because that answer naturally extends to what we would do in the case when it does converge. And that latter question is foundational (and unaddressed) in optimization: should we output the last set of parameter estimates or the best set of parameter estimates according to the objective function?

In monotonic sort of optimization routines the two are equivalent. In stuff likes stochastic approximations, however, there are good reasons for either. For instance, in non convex optimization SGD might so happen as to land at a high point of one hill but later jump away and end up converging at the top of a lower hill. Do we output the parameters leading to the higher point—which is likely not even a local optima—or do we output the local optima that we converged too?

For now I think the best solution is to output a warning if (1) the maximum number of iterations is reached; and/or (2) the ELBO is higher at a set of parameters which isn’t the last set.

messages.subject: Some improvements to StataStan
messages.body_plain:
I've ironed out some kinks in StataStan, mainly:
1) you can watch progress almost live in the Stata results window; this wasn't possible before in any Stata version under Windows
2) you can write your Stan model code inside a comment block in the Stata .do file, and leave Stata to find it (without having to hard-code the name of the .do file itself); this is a step up on John Thompson's Stata-to-BUGS commands (but you don't have to do it that way - see stan-example.do for the options)

So far so good in Linux and Windows. But if you know of any Stata people with Macs, please ask them to try it out:
https://github.com/stan-dev/statastan/tree/alpha-test
I need to know that it behaves on all three Stata OSs before we call it v0.1.

Cheers
Robert

Hi Bob!

The repeated autodiffing of the system function could be a possibility for optimization where a user-defined sensitivity system would also help, sure (or caching of the autodiff stack if this is possible).

Having an event capable ODE integrator helps in the following way: Currently, I step through the data set from event to event and each time I restart the integrator with a new initial state which is state of the system function at the time point when a new event is encountered.

Since the event history is fixed with the data as is the initial state at time point 0, the sensitivities for the initial time point is not needed if the integrator were to process things with events in a single sweep.

Concretely, in a PK system with dosing: The initial state is always 0 in all compartments (no drug ever administered). The history of dosing events is fixed with the data and hence no sensitivities are needed for the initials. However in the current design I have to integrate in steps and restart the integrator at each dosing event with the initial set to the amounts in the compartments at the time of the dosing event.

Not having the initials as parameters considerably reduces the coupled system size.

Sebastian

messages.subject: cvode working & user-specified sensitivities give huge performance boost
messages.subject_clean: cvode working & user-specified sensitivities give huge performance boost
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I resurrected Toms cvode branch and found out why it was performing so bad: cvode was built with cmake which DISABLES by default compiler options. So setting compilation flags right did make cvode run fast. Tom did a lot of quirks which I did not follow in order to enable a Jacobian calculation of the coupled system which I disabled.

On the example benchmark on a 2-cmt model enabling cvode made it possible to solve; before Stan was frozen quickly after the first draws.

Next, I wanted to try out what user-defined sensitivities would bring in terms of speed: The result was a thrilling speedup of more than 10x (i.e. the display of gradient evaluation said 0.08s with "vanilla" cvode while it said 0s for the system with user-defined sensitivities).

The way I implemented the user defined sensitivities did not change the function signature of integrate_ode! So I hope this change can go into Stan as no user code will be affected, I just generalized the behavior: The idea is that the size of the y0 vector gives me N, the number of equations in the base system. Now passing things into the coupled_ode_system creates the coupled system and the size of that system is then N_coupled=N + N*(N+M); M being number of parameters and I assume that parameters and initials vary. Now, inside integrate_ode I simply call the user supplied system function f once. IF the returned vector has size N_coupled I know that the user was so kind to provide symbolically the full sensitivity system which I then integrate. The decoupling operation is still being done by the "old" coupled_system.

Stan occasionally calls the integrate_ode function during sampling with parameters and initials fixed which surprised me, but one can detect this situation and then give correct output.

This nice thing about the implementation is that no user facing code needs to be touched and the functionality has been extended.

The 2-cmt system with oral dosing (N=3 ODES, M=4 parameters => N_coupled=24) can now be solved for 10 patients with each ~70 observations (two random effects) in only 335 s (244s / 91s)! Stan 2.7.0 froze completely on iteration 3.

Getting those sensitivities is a pain, but this can be automized by using some scripting language which is capable to do easily symbolic differentiation and the write out a integrate_ode function...if includes were to come some time then this approach would be more user friendly.

Looking forward for feedback on this - I must say, I am very excited.

Sebastian

Hi Bob!

I think my case here confirms the anticipated problem of Boosts solver with stiff parameter draws leading to a freeze.

Your understanding of how I handle user-specified sensitivities is correct. I.e. let y0 be the vector of initials of size N (number of base equations), also let f be the user-supplied system function which returns dydt. For the case of user-specified sensitivities, the system function f returns a dydt vector which is much longer, just as long as all needed sensitivities, N + N * (N+M); M being the number of parameters. My thought was that no user code gets invalid by doing this and the behavior is simply generalized. So modifications to Stan should be minimal (testing wise, doc wise, etc.); however, the impact is huge (>10X) on speed.

Now, if you want a different function signature, then you could go with returned matrices - no need for tuples for which we have to wait a while. I mean, the user could define a system function f which returns a matrix with N rows (number of equations) and 1 + N + M columns. This would require a little bit more work as integrate_ode needs an overload (and possibly more changes I am not aware of).

For the approach of an extended return vector, I have by now a good idea of how to code this nicely in the coupled_ode object. If this idea should be further explored, I am happy to provide a patch which could be against the current develop branch of stan math.

Moreover, if the decision is to go with cvode, then it would make sense to consider cvodes (yes, an extra s). This is cvode with sensitivity analysis, which I think is exactly what Stan needs and possibly more efficient than autodiffing the base system in every function call to the system function. Specifically, cvode solves the problem y' = f(t,y) with f(t0) = y0 while cvodes solves y' = f(t,y,p) with f(t0) = y0(p). So you pass into cvodes a function which takes y, t and theta (theta = p being the parameters). The documentation then advertises that cvodes calculates the needed sensitivities. If it provides really everything, I don't know, but exploring this makes sense once sundials is going into Stan. BTW, sundials is actively developed (this year two releases) which I consider a good sign.

I am really looking forward to this!

Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I just skimmed through the cvodes documentation and I am convinced that this is the right approach. cvodes is specifically tailored for a sensitivity analysis as Stan needs it - and the documentation warns against augmenting the base ODE system as this does not take advantage of the fact that the sensitivities are effectively a linearization of the base system and also dramatically increases the system size. Now, the manual also highly recommends to provide a Jacobian for the base system (or at least a crude estimate). This is to enable pre-conditioning which speedups the solving process. However, now the Jacobian of the base system is needed here - which we can get from Stan using autodiff!!!

I really hope those windows installation issues don't stop us here from using sundials, but I am starting to believe that Stan can provide an extremely fast implementation for solving ODEs out of the box; since employing cvodes and providing the Jacobian via auto-diff will give very good performance.

I will try to get a prototype of this up and running. BTW, this would of course remove the need for user-sensitivities...

Cheers,
Sebastian

Just saw that I claimed that user-sensitivities would not be needed given the use of cvodes. This of course simply wrong, sorry.

In summary, the solving process would be greatly speed up by using cvode and if possible cvodes (in fact the manual of cvodes specifically mentions parameter estimation as on of the applications of their cvodes suite). - system function returning a longer than usual vector
- system function returning a matrix
- an extra integrate_ode function which takes in addition to the system function, the system sensitivity function as argument. This last option would be most suitable for cvodes.

Sorry for any confusion.

Sebastian

messages.subject: Further ODE speedup opportunity with reduced sensitivity system?
messages.subject_clean: Further ODE speedup opportunity with reduced sensitivity system?
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I had an idea which seems to turn out very attractive for complex ODE modeling. In PKPD modeling and I believe generally in complex structural ODE modeling where Bayes is very attractive to use due to available physical knowledge of the system, the situation is very often that quite a number of ODEs N are needed to describe the system, but only very few No << N are observed and enter the likelihood.

In my example I am considering, I have a 2-cmt oral dosing PK system which has N=3, but only concentrations from the second compartement are observed and enter the likelihood. Currently Stan calculates the sensitivities with respect to parameters and initials for all N equations - but only Ns (=1 in my case) enter the likelihood. So the full coupled system in this case (M=4 parameters) is 24. Now, I thought why not reduce the coupled system to only what is needed, which is in this case 7 sensitivities for the second equation and 3 for the base system, so in total only 10 equations to solve.

I applied this idea to the cvode branch I worked out with the user-specified sensitivities and the results I get as parameters estimates are exactly the same. The theoretical speedup should be 2.4, but I end up getting 1.7:

Full coupled system, 24 ODEs (250 warmup/250 iterations):
#  Elapsed Time: 207.61 seconds (Warm-up)
#                76.71 seconds (Sampling)
#                284.32 seconds (Total)

Reduced coupled system, 10 ODEs (same iterations):
#  Elapsed Time: 122.37 seconds (Warm-up)
#                46.28 seconds (Sampling)
#                168.65 seconds (Total)

The advantage of this approach grows quadratic in N! I know that many modelers love to come up with tons of euqations to model their system, but only very few of those quantities are observed such that this (little) optimization will have a large impact, I think. It would enable to apply Stan to very complex systems with few observed outcomes - a typical situation from what I am aware of.

Best,
Sebastian
